newsitem.title: LATVIA: New Latvian finmin says balanced budget key task.
newsitem.headline: New Latvian finmin says balanced budget key task.

text.p: New Latvian Finance Minister Vassily Melnik said on Thursday that his main task would be to make sure that the 1997 budget remained balanced.
The budget recorded a deficit of nearly 40 million lat in 1996 and 90 million lat in 1995.
"My main task now is to carry out the law on the balanced budget, passed by parliament in December last year," Melnik told a news conference after parliament backed his appointment.
Melnik, a 29-year-old businessman, earlier gained the backing of 44 MPs of 71 present in the 100-seat chamber.
A balanced 1997 budget, passed amid political controversy, is part of Latvia's commitment to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in return for IMF credits.
Melnik said he would probably add funds to the welfare sphere if there was any surplus cash in the budget.
Melnik belongs to the largest party in the six-party coalition government, the Democratic Party Saimnieks.
During the debate on the 1997 budget, it backed an increase in teachers' and doctors' salaries and a rise in pensions.
Saimnieks head Ziedonis Chevers said the party still wanted to boost funding for the welfare sector but would do so only if the funds were available.
Melnik's appointment came amid controversy and allegations he was under investigation for a conflict of interest. But prosecutors said he had not broken an anti-corruption law.
President Guntis Ulmanis had earlier called on MPs not to back Melnik's candidature and the Peasant's Union, one of the government coalition parties, largely voted against Melniks.
"The most important thing was that the prime minister trusts me. I was his advisor during the time Shkele was acting finance minister," Melnik said.
Latvia had been without a finance minister since October, when Aivar Kreituss resigned after being dismissed from his political party.
Prime Minister Andris Shkele took over as acting finance minister and steered the 1997 balanced budget through parliament.
